metadata.title: A Cross-National Examination of Teachers’ Multicultural Self-Efficacy: Can Multicultural Education in Initial Teacher Education and Professional Development Make a Difference?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data with a two-stage random sampling design (schools sampled within each country/economy, then teachers sampled within schools). The manuscript reports that teachers completed a questionnaire and that the analysis used multilevel modeling with teachers nested within countries. However, the paper does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is multilevel modeling of questionnaire composite scores (not ML training), the weighting strategy is not documented; readers should treat the results as conditional on the authors’ implemented estimation approach rather than assuming population-representative weighted estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables (TMSE and TSE) are constructed from Likert-scale questionnaire items and analyzed as composite scale scores, not as PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. The paper explicitly states that listwise deletion was used to exclude missing values, so missing-data handling is documented for the analytic sample. Therefore, PV-specific handling is not part of the methodology for this study.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 lower secondary teachers, then excluded Russia, Spain, and Iceland due to questionnaire administration or data availability issues. Further excluded teachers with incomplete responses. Additionally, the analytic sample was restricted to teachers who had previously taught in culturally diverse classrooms (because TALIS 2018 only surveyed TMSE for that subgroup). Final analytic sample comprised 65,978 teachers across 45 countries/economies after listwise deletion of missing values.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teachers; TMSE scale from 5 items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel Model A: TSE related to TMSE (β = 0.473, p < .001). Pseudo R2 of TSE = 40% (implying 60% of TMSE variance unexplained). ICC (country effect) = 16.59%. Control effects: female teachers higher TMSE (β = 0.015, p < .01); teaching experience negative (β = −0.002, p < .001); degree status not related (β = 0.009, p = .?? not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged Teacher self-efficacy (TSE), Gender (female), Teaching experience (years), and Degree status (master’s+) to predict Multicultural self-efficacy (TMSE composite score), finding that TSE was strongly and positively associated with TMSE (β = 0.473, p < .001) while TMSE remained largely distinct (60% of variance unexplained by TSE). This indicates that strengthening general teacher self-efficacy alone is likely insufficient to fully build multicultural self-efficacy, so teacher training should include targeted multicultural components rather than relying only on broad efficacy development.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for lower secondary teachers who had previously taught in culturally diverse classrooms, excluding Russia, Spain, and Iceland and removing teachers with incomplete responses. Multilevel modeling was used with teachers nested within countries, and TMSE was measured via five Likert items (composited into a mean scale). In Model A, teacher self-efficacy (TSE) showed a strong positive association with TMSE (β = 0.473, p < .001) with a pseudo R2 of 40%, yet 60% of TMSE variance remained unexplained, supporting TMSE as distinct from general efficacy. In Model B, multicultural education in initial teacher education (ITE) and professional development (PD) were both positively related to TMSE (β = 0.129 and 0.123, respectively, p < .001), but the combined explained variance was small (pseudo R2 ≈ 7.14%). The paper uses listwise deletion for missing values and does not report any survey-weight or PV handling because the outcomes are questionnaire composites rather than PV-based achievement scores; additionally, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
